outputs.L1:
For eight months he lay in bed, turning over the difference between "the bell rings" and "he rings the bell." Did those two rings *sound* different? Did the invisible disturbance—the bell's vibration beating against the air, a field effect—shift according to the ringer's will? This, he thought, was the smallest difference the human mind could hold, or almost hold—the thought slipping away even as it was thought, a penny rolling toward the horizon, and so to sleep . . .

He could not rise. It became clear to him that he was the murderer. Everyone knows this.

A man stands at a podium, reading from his notes. In the audience, people nod in immaculate suits, women and men alike. When I finish, someone will transcribe what I have said into speech. It will bear no resemblance to my notes. He is merely THE THING that exists between his notes and his speech. This seems only fair—that he should be the air itself.

Some of the women wear hats trimmed with feathers, wild and incandescent. Among the audience sits a boy named B—not the letter, not the note. Another sound, neither letter nor note—
outputs.L2:
For eight months he remained bedridden, consumed by a single question: is there any sonic distinction between "the bell rings" and "he rings the bell"? Do these phrases produce distinguishable sounds? Consider the bell's vibrations—that unseen disturbance rippling through air, a phenomenon of pure field effect—does this physical event alter depending on whether an agent wills it into being? He believed this represented the tiniest conceivable gap the human intellect might grasp (or nearly grasp, since the concept always slipped from cognition's fingers, like a coin rolling endlessly toward some distant horizon, dissolving finally into sleep). Rising from bed proved impossible. Eventually it dawned on him: he was guilty of murder. Everybody understands this.

Picture a man behind a lectern, reciting from prepared notes. Below him, an audience of impeccably dressed figures—men and women alike—nod in unison. Once I finish speaking, someone will render my words into transcribed speech, though it won't match what I'd written beforehand. He exists merely as the medium connecting his written words to his spoken ones. Justly so—let him embody that intervening air itself.

Scattered among the women are hats crowned with feathers, untamed and glowing with strange luminescence. Somewhere in that crowd sits a child called B—not the letter B, not a musical note either, but something else: a sound that belongs to neither category—
outputs.L3:
For eight months, the man did not leave his bed. His body had surrendered to some illness of will or nerve, but his mind would not rest, circling instead around a single, maddening question: does "the bell rings" differ from "he rings the bell"? Is there a distinction—not merely grammatical, but physical, sonic—between these two utterances? He imagined the bell itself, its bronze curve trembling in the air, and wondered whether its vibrations might actually change shape depending on whether the sound arose of its own accord or was summoned by a human hand. Did intention alter the wave? Did will leave a fingerprint on frequency?

This distinction, he came to believe, was the finest thread the human mind could almost hold—a filament of meaning so delicate that the moment one reached for it, it slipped away, rolling off into the dark like a dropped penny chasing its own glint across the floor. He would almost grasp it. Almost understand why the world allowed this asymmetry between the bell that rings and the man who rings it. And then it was gone, and he had to begin again from stillness.

Lying there, unable to lift himself, he arrived slowly at a second, stranger certainty: that he was a murderer. Not that he had killed someone in the way the word usually implies, but that the guilt of it clung to him regardless, a truth apparently self-evident to everyone but him—until now. He felt it settle into his chest with the calm horror of remembering something one has always known but never said aloud. No one had accused him. No one needed to. It was simply understood, the way weather is understood, the way a name fits a face.

Elsewhere—perhaps in another fold of this same unraveling mind—a man stood at a podium. Before him lay notes he was about to speak, knowing that whatever was written down afterward, whatever transcription would follow his voice, would bear only a distorted resemblance to what he actually said. He did not think of himself as the source of meaning, nor even as its vessel. He thought of himself as merely the air between the note and its utterance—the invisible medium through which intention passed on its way to becoming sound, and then, inevitably, on its way to becoming something else entirely once written down. He was not the message. He was the space the message moved through.

The room around him was full of people dressed with unnerving precision—suits without a single crease out of place, women beneath wide hats crowned with feathers that trembled slightly as they breathed. Among this audience, near the back or perhaps near the front, a boy named B sat very still. Around him drifted sounds that belonged to no alphabet and to no scale—not letters, not notes, but something suspended between the two, as if language and music had both dissolved into a third, formless thing that only he could hear, and even he was not sure he was hearing it at all.
outputs.L4:
For eight months he did not leave the bed. This was not illness in any diagnosable sense, though the doctors were summoned twice and left twice with the particular helplessness of men trained to treat bodies confronting instead a mind that had lodged itself, immovably, in a question of grammar.

The question was this: when the bell rings, and when someone rings the bell, is the sound produced in each case the same sound, or does the phrasing itself—the intransitive construction against the transitive—reach down into the acoustic event and alter it, however minutely, however unverifiably? He would lie there through the grey hours turning the two sentences over as one turns a coin, looking for the seam where they diverged. *The bell rings.* No agent, no hand, no intention—only the pure occurrence, the world simply doing what it does, sound arising as weather arises, as light arrives. *He rings the bell.* Here suddenly there is a will behind the event, a subject pushing through the verb into the object, and the sound—was it not now a different sound, freighted with intention, no longer simply happening but being *made* to happen?

He understood, with the particular clarity available only to the bedridden, that this was perhaps the smallest distinction the mind could hold without it dissolving into nothing at all—smaller than the distinction between similar shades of color, smaller than the gap between two nearly identical notes played on the same string. It was the field-effect boundary itself, the membrane between occurrence and will, and he had made it his entire occupation to stand at that membrane and feel for its thickness. Some nights he believed he had found it—a barely perceptible shift, as if the transitive sentence carried a shadow the intransitive one lacked, a residue of the hand in the sound of the metal. Other nights the distinction evaporated entirely and he was left holding two identical sentences that meant, that could only ever mean, exactly the same bell, exactly the same ringing, and his entire eight months revealed themselves as an elaborate structure built on nothing, a cathedral of grammar erected over an absence.

It was on one such night, when the distinction had failed him completely, that the guilt arrived. Not guilt over anything he had done—he had done nothing, that was rather the point—but guilt over the doing of the inquiry itself, as though to spend eight months prone in a room asking whether a bell's ringing was willed or merely occurring was itself an act requiring justification, and one he could not provide. He began, then, the long interior indictment: that he had wasted the season, that he had used philosophy as a way of not living, that the question of the bell was only ever a disguise for the question of himself—whether he, lying there, was ringing or being rung, whether his own inertia was a decision or simply the absence of one, whether he had *chosen* this stillness or had merely, like the bell, been struck by something and left to vibrate until the vibration ceased on its own. The self-accusation did not resolve the metaphysical question; it merely absorbed it, folded the grammar of the bell into the grammar of his own culpability until the two were indistinguishable, until *he rings* and *he is guilty* sat side by side in his mind as versions of the same unbearable sentence.

And then, without any transition he could later reconstruct, he was standing before an audience. Perhaps this was imagined, perhaps it was memory retrieved from some earlier life before the bed, perhaps it was neither and simply the mind's way of discharging what it could no longer hold in the abstract. He was speaking—reading, rather, from notes he had written in some prior state of composure, notes now transcribed by another hand into the minutes of the occasion, into whatever official record such occasions produce. And he noticed, standing there, that he himself was neither the notes nor the transcription. He was the interval between them. The written word had existed before he opened his mouth; the transcribed word would exist after he closed it; and he, standing at the lectern, moving his lips, producing breath shaped into sound shaped into sense, was only ever the medium through which one fixed thing became another fixed thing—was, in fact, nothing more than air. Air that had passed briefly between two kinds of ink.

This seemed, suddenly, to answer the question of the bell, though not in any way he could have anticipated. For if he himself, delivering speech, was merely the transitional air between the note and its transcription—if his voice added nothing, subtracted nothing, but only carried the words across the small terrifying gap between one fixation of meaning and the next—then perhaps the bell too was never rung nor ringing in any way that mattered, but was simply the site where an intention became an event became a record, and the grammar he had spent eight months interrogating was not describing two different sounds at all. It was describing the same unlocatable passage, the same evaporating agency, that he now recognized in himself: not a thing, not a self, not a will fixed anywhere, but a kind of air moving between positions, taking the shape of intention only long enough to be mistaken for it, before dispersing into whatever came next.

He understood then that he would probably remain in the room a while longer. Not because the question had resolved, but because he had finally located where such questions live—not in the bell, not in the man who strikes it, but in the thin, unnamable interval between the striking and the sound, where meaning is neither made nor found but merely, briefly, passed through.
outputs.L5:
# SOUND

Did you ever stop to consider how much your world would change without sound? For most of us, sound is such a constant companion that we barely notice it until it's gone.

Think about it: the hum of a refrigerator, the distant bark of a dog, the rustle of leaves in wind. These background noises create a sense of place and presence that we rarely acknowledge consciously. For many people, silence itself can feel unsettling—not peaceful, but almost eerie.

Did you know that sound is simply vibration traveling through a medium, whether air, water, or solid matter? For sound to exist at all, there must be something for those vibrations to move through. This is why space, despite being filled with dramatic events like exploding stars, is utterly silent. There's no medium to carry the waves.

For musicians, sound is raw material—something to be shaped, layered, and transformed into emotion. For engineers, it's a technical challenge involving frequencies, amplitudes, and acoustics. For someone who has lost their hearing, sound might represent a memory, a phantom sense that still shapes how they perceive the world through vibration and visual cues.

Did the pandemic change how we listen? For many, months of quieter streets and grounded planes revealed a soundscape long buried under urban noise. Birdsong seemed louder, more present, more meaningful.

For all its complexity, sound remains one of the most underappreciated aspects of human experience. Did you notice the sounds around you today? For a moment, try really listening. You might discover a world you didn't know was there.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem about a bedridden man obsessing over the subtle difference between "the bell rings" and "he rings the bell," blending linguistic philosophy with dreamlike guilt.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Grammar of the Bell

He has been lying here long enough that the ceiling has become a page, and on it, endlessly, the same sentence rewrites itself: *the bell rings.*

No subject but the bell. No hand behind it. The bell rings the way rain falls, the way blood insists through a body without asking permission—an event without an author, weather with a clapper in it. He likes this sentence. He can lie inside it the way he lies inside himself, undisturbed, uncomplicit, a man to whom things merely happen.

But then the other sentence comes, always from the hallway, always in his mother's voice or the voice of someone who resembles her the way fog resembles a person standing at a distance: *he rings the bell.*

There it is. The hand. The intention curling out from the wrist like smoke that knows exactly where it's going. Someone did this. Someone reached, and pulled, and meant it, and the meaning doesn't dissolve afterward — it stays, hardens, becomes a small fossil lodged behind the sternum.

He tries to decide which sentence is true and understands, somewhere in the mattress-deep hours of the afternoon, that this is not a grammatical question. It is the difference between *it happened* and *I did it* — between the weather and the crime.

The room fills with the sound anyway, subjectless, oceanic, and he cannot tell if he is the bell or the hand or the small guilty boy who is always, in every version of the dream, standing just behind the door he was told not to open.

He remembers a bell from years ago — the sound arriving before he could ask who made it. He remembers his own hand, once, closing around a rope he had no permission to touch, and the terrible clarity of the *he rings the bell* that followed him out of that room like a verdict.

Now, ceiling-bound, unable to verify which sentence describes his condition — the passive tense of illness (*it happens to him*) or the active tense of some old, unconfessed thing (*he did this, he made this, this is his*) — he begins to suspect that grammar was invented as a mercy. So the world could be split into what merely occurs and what someone is responsible for. So the guilty could rest sometimes in the passive voice, could say *the bell rings* and mean *I am not the one who has to answer for the sound.*

But the sound keeps insisting on a subject.

He listens for the bell as if it might clarify itself, as if this time it might arrive already labeled — *this one has no one behind it* — but it never does. It only rings, ownerless and accusing at once, the way memory rings, the way the body rings with old, uncashed guilt, the sentence never finishing, never deciding whether he is the one being rung for, or the one, somewhere far back, who reached out first and pulled.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental piece of fiction in the style of Gertrude Stein or Beckett, exploring sound, language, and identity through a fragmented narrative involving a man who cannot get out of bed.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Bed That Is Not Getting Up**

The man is in the bed. The bed is in the man. This is not a saying, this is a fact that is not a fact, this is a thing that continues.

He says, I will get up. He says it the way one says a word until it is not a word. Get up. Get up. Getup. Getupgetup. The word wears down like a stone in a shoe, like a shoe that has forgotten it is a shoe, like forgetting.

There is a morning. There is a morning in the room and the morning is the same morning as yesterday's morning, wearing the same coat, using the same key, and the man says, this is not the same morning, and the morning does not answer because mornings do not answer, they only arrive and arrive and arrive.

*

Listen. There is a sound. The sound is the sound of the man not getting up. It is a small sound. It is the sound a person makes when they are being a person and not doing the thing that persons do, which is get up, which is stand, which is walk into a day and call it Tuesday or call it nothing, call it the day the plumbing complained, call it the day.

He is called Frank. He is not called Frank. Somewhere a woman calls a name into a hallway and the name might be his name and it might not be, and the not-getting-up continues whether or not the name is his.

Frank. Frank. Are you.

Am I, he says. Am I is a question the bed keeps asking underneath him, in the springs, in the small conversations the springs have with the weight of him lying there being a weight, being a shape, being the shape of not getting up.

*

Here is the room. The room has a window. The window has a light in it, coming from a sun, or from a lamp on a pole outside, the light does not specify, the light is simply the doing of light, which is arriving and touching the wall and being ignored.

The man in the bed thinks: I am the one who is not getting up.

Then he thinks: someone is thinking that I am the one who is not getting up.

Then he thinks nothing, and the nothing is comfortable, the nothing has the shape of the blanket, and he pulls the nothing up around the not-getting-up and the two of them, the nothing and the not-getting-up, are warm together in the bed that is also warm, or cold, the temperature is not the point, the point is the pulling up.

*

Voice one: Get up.
Voice two: I am up. I am up in the sense that up is a direction and I am facing it.
Voice one: Facing is not up.
Voice two: No. Facing is not up. Up is up. I am not up.

There are two voices and they might be one voice divided the way a road divides, into a road that goes and a road that also goes, both going, neither arriving, and the man in the bed listens to the voices dividing and thinks, that is not my voice, that is the voice of the not-getting-up speaking through the shape of my mouth.

*

Say the word bed. Bed bed bed. Say it until it means water. Say it until it means nothing, until the *b* is only a shutting of the lips and the *ed* is only a small ending that keeps not ending. Bed. The word holds him the way the bed holds him, both of them made of the same waiting.

He thinks of his legs. His legs are elsewhere. His legs have gone on without the rest of him, walking somewhere in a field that is not this room, and he is here, the part of him that remained, the part that is mostly a listening, a lying-there, a being-had by the mattress.

*

It is afternoon. It was morning and now without transition it is afternoon, the way in a story time simply announces itself, "and now it is afternoon," without the courtesy of showing the getting-there.

The man says: I will get up in the afternoon.

The afternoon says nothing, being an afternoon, being only the accumulation of a certain slant of light, and slants itself further towards evening while he watches it, or does not watch it, watching not being required for the slanting to occur.

*

Someone knocks. Knock knock. The knock is a small hammer of sound against the door and the door holds the sound the way skin holds a slap, briefly, then lets it go into the rest of the house, into the pipes, into the other rooms where other not-getting-ups might or might not be happening.

Is he in there, someone asks, someone who is perhaps the woman, perhaps not.

He is in there, someone answers, someone who is perhaps himself, saying it about himself as if from outside, as if he had already left the bed and was standing in the hallway describing the man who had not.

*

He begins a list. Reasons.

One, the weight.
Two, the weight of the weight.
Three, a rehearsal of standing, done lying down, which is not standing, which is only the idea of a leg moving, an idea with no leg attached.
Four, the day does not require him specifically.
Five, the bed requires him specifically.
Six, he has begun to be the kind of man about whom it is said, he does not get up.
Seven, being that kind of man is itself a getting up of a kind, a standing into a name.

He stops the list because the list is getting up without him, the list is walking into the day in his place, dressed in his reasons, and he watches it go.

*

Evening. He says the word evening and the word sits down on the end of the day like a person sitting on the end of a bed, and now there are two of them not getting up, the evening and the man, keeping company, saying nothing, the room going dim in the ordinary way that rooms go dim, without asking permission, without apology.

He thinks: tomorrow.

The word arrives, small and round, tomorrow, and he holds it the way he held bed, the way he held Frank, turning it until it is only sound, until it means a bed also, until it means nothing but the shape of a mouth opening and closing on an *o*.

Tomorrow, he says, I will get up.

The bed says nothing.
The room says nothing.
Somewhere the woman turns off a light in another part of the house, and the not-getting-up, unwitnessed now, continues, quietly, the way water continues to be wet even in the dark, even when there is no one there to say so.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, avant-garde literary passage that moves between a man paralyzed by a linguistic puzzle and a scene of someone giving a speech at a podium, using repetition and sudden tonal shifts.
counterfactuals.output:
# Fragments at the Threshold

The man sat with the word in his mouth like a stone he could not swallow or spit. *Threshold.* He had said it forty times. *Threshold, threshold, threshold*—until the sounds detached from meaning and became only weather, only the sound wind makes finding a crack in a window frame.

He thought: a threshold is the place you are not yet through.

He thought: a threshold is the place you are already leaving.

At the podium, she gripped both edges of the wood like a woman holding the sides of a boat.

"We stand," she said, "at a threshold."

The audience nodded. Someone coughed. The word moved through the room the way water moves through a hose left in the sun—warm, expected, going somewhere else.

The man, elsewhere, entirely elsewhere, tried again: *threshold.* He tried to remember what a door was for. A door is for closing. A door is for the shape of a body passing through it and the room deciding, after, that it had always been empty.

"We stand at a threshold," she said again, because repetition is how the important things get buried, or built—she could not remember which metaphor she'd chosen, walking in.

The man's hand, on the table, did not move. His hand was a threshold too. Between the wanting and the reaching. Between *I will* and the long grey afterward where intentions go to be forgiven.

"This is not a threshold," she said suddenly, veering, the room tightening around the change like a throat. "This is the room after the threshold. We are already inside whatever we were afraid of."

The audience did not nod this time.

The man opened his mouth. The stone was gone. In its place: nothing, a held door, a version of silence that resembled a word about to happen.

Outside, actual wind found an actual window.

It did not knock. It had already been let in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a stream-of-consciousness text exploring the phenomenology of sound and speech—how vibration, will, and meaning intersect—ending in a scene where notes are transformed into spoken words before an audience.
counterfactuals.output:
Sound first as pressure, as air displaced, as the body's drum-taut membrane trembling before mind ever names it music or noise—vibration arriving wordless, insistent, a pulse against the eardrum that asks nothing and simply is, until the mind leans in and says: listen, there is something here, and in that leaning the raw wave becomes a signal, becomes almost-meaning, becomes the threshold where physics and psyche shake hands.

And I wonder how much of speaking is will and how much is release—the diaphragm's involuntary heave, the vocal folds snapping together twelve hundred times a second without my ever choosing each snap, and yet somehow I choose to speak, I decide the shape of the exhale, I aim the breath through the narrow gate of larynx and tongue and teeth until it comes out as *word*—as if intention were a hand cupped around chaos, coaxing it into form, the way a potter's fingers don't create the clay but only give it a shape it was already capable of holding.

Before the word there is the tone—the hum, the drone, the sung note that carries feeling without carrying sense, the way a mother's lullaby means everything and says nothing, the way grief groans and joy peals and the body knows these registers before language arrives to translate them, to betray them a little, to make them portable and shareable at the cost of some of their rawness—for meaning is always a compression, a flattening of the felt wave into the discrete packet, the phoneme, the syllable that can be repeated identically by another throat and still (this is the miracle) still land as something like the same feeling.

I think of the vibration traveling out from the body like a ring in water, touching other bodies, other eardrums, and how strange that my private trembling can become your trembling too, that sound is the medium of a kind of communion that sight can't quite achieve, because sound enters through no chosen aperture—you cannot close your ears the way you close your eyes—sound simply arrives, invasive and intimate at once, and this is why a scream can violate and a lullaby can heal and the difference is not in the physics but in the will behind the breath, the shape the mind gave the air before releasing it.

And now, here, before them—the room quiets, the throat clears, the diaphragm gathers itself like a held breath before a dive—and what was hum becomes tone, what was tone becomes shaped tone, what was shaped tone bends at last into the sharp architecture of consonants, into words that carry not just feeling but reference, argument, story—the notes I might have simply sung dissolve into the harder, more precise music of language, and I open my mouth, and the vibration that was only mine becomes, in this instant, everyone's:

"Thank you all for being here tonight."
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of poetic prose that fuses themes of guilt, invisible causality, and the instability of language, incorporating imagery of bells, feathers, and a boy named "B" who is not a letter or a note.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of B

The bell does not know it is a bell until it is rung, and even then it forgets—the sound leaving no residue of intention, no fingerprint of the hand that pulled the rope. This is how guilt works: retroactive, uncertain, always arriving after the fact to claim what it did not witness.

B was a boy before he was a letter. Before he was mistaken for a note held too long in some minor key, he was simply a small weight in a doorway, casting the shadow that shadows cast—unremarkable, temporary, alive.

*Say his name*, they said, as if language could hold water, as if a syllable were a vessel and not a sieve. B, they wrote, and the letter stood up in the sentence like a tombstone that had wandered from its grave, looking for the body it was meant to mark. But he was not a symbol. He would not consent to standing for anything.

The feathers came after—always after, the way guilt comes after, the way sound comes after the bell's cold iron mouth opens and closes on nothing. They fell from a bird no one saw fly overhead, or from a pillow torn in a fight that happened in another house, another year. They fell the way blame falls: without origin, without owner, simply *arriving*, already scattered, already past the point where anyone could gather them back into wings.

*I didn't*, someone says. *I didn't mean.* But meaning is a bell that rings backward, calling the clapper toward a silence it will never quite reach. We ring and ring, and the sound moves through walls we didn't know were there, into rooms where a boy sits who is not a letter, not a note, not the small ghost of grammar haunting our mouths when we try to explain what happened, what we did, what merely occurred in our vicinity like weather, like feathers, like the long, unspooling doubt of a bell that has already, always, been rung.

He looks up. He is only himself. The room fills with a sound no one made on purpose, and it does not stop being his name, and it does not stop, also, being nothing at all—b, breath, a shape the mouth makes before it decides what it's guilty of.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
